The task: a Gray-Scott pattern is observed at step 300 through a sparse set of pixels, and the Diffusion Controller returns a state at step 50 that grows back into it.
The answer is judged by the re-simulation error, the distance between the observed pattern and what the solver grows from the answer.
It is not judged by closeness to the true start: many different starts grow into the same pattern, and a simpler one is preferred over the true one.

The method follows DiffusionPDE [@huang2024diffusionpde].
A U-Net denoiser [@karras2022elucidating] learns what consistent pairs of early and late states look like.
Starting from pure noise, a draw is steered towards the observed pixels while the denoiser keeps the pair physically plausible.
Eight draws are made, the one that fits the observations best is kept, and a final polish runs 150 gradient steps through the solver.
Examples are on [Pattern Forcing](../gray-scott-inversion/index.qmd).

## Results

On 16 × 16 grids with 50 observed pixels, the best method regrows the pattern almost exactly, and no pattern dies.
Most of the gain comes from choosing among draws and from the polish, not from the network: a single draw is off by 0.426, and simply looking up the best of all 359 training starts already reaches 0.128.

{{< include charts/ladder.html >}}

The same method scales to larger grids when the number of observed pixels grows with the grid.

{{< include charts/grids.html >}}

The recovered start is not the true one: its error stays at 0.20–0.22 on every grid, however many pixels are observed.
That is expected, since the observed pattern does not determine its past, and by the rule above it is not a failure.
The patterns themselves make the past hard to see: a growing pattern first shrinks to its smallest area, around step 125, and only then spreads again.
Placing the 49 observed pixels on a regular grid instead of at random lowered the error further, from 0.0067 to 0.0021 on 8 scenes (better on 7 of 8, p = 0.07).

## How the data were simulated

The Gray-Scott model has an activator u and a substrate v.
Scenes were simulated on a square with no-flux boundaries and a grid spacing of 2 length units; diffusion is solved exactly in a cosine basis and the reaction by an explicit step, with time step 1.218.
Each scene starts from a random field: u is half the positive part of a Gaussian random field and v is 1 everywhere.
The states at steps 50 and 300 are stored, and a scene is kept only if it is still patterned at step 300, about half of them.
The 16 × 16 model trains on 359 such scenes; the 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 models on streams of 20,000 scenes each, with U²-Nets of 3.7 and 6.0 million parameters.

Parameter choices:

- **Feed a = 0.02842, kill b = 0.05368.** Kept from the earlier project this one grew from; the point lies just above the fold below which no pattern survives (a > 4(a+b)², ratio 1.054).
- **Diffusivities 0.3 for u, 1.0 for v.** The activator must diffuse more slowly than the substrate.
- **Grid spacing 2.** A spacing of 4 pinned strokes to the grid axes; 2 matches a much finer reference within about 10%.
- **Time step 1.218.** Set for accuracy, dt·(a+b) ≤ 0.1; the diffusion step is stable at any size.

Which U-Net: on this task the U²-Net prior beat a plain U-Net (one draw 0.426 against 0.562) and was used from then on.

## Changing the training starts

How the training starts are generated matters more than which network is used.
An early 16 × 16 study (steps 50 to 100) trained the same model on three kinds of start: random fields, a few Gaussian blobs, or both.

{{< include charts/ic.html >}}

The transfer is lopsided.
A model trained on blobs recovers random-field starts nearly as well as a specialist, because by step 50 a random field looks like many small blobs.
A model trained on random fields cannot draw one large smooth blob, so it fails on blob starts.
Mixing the two lost to the blob specialist on both kinds of start.
At step 300, a U²-Net retrained on simple blob and line starts reached 0.083, no better than searching for those starts directly (0.068, below).

## Parameter fields instead of a start

The same denoiser can instead return the feed, kill and diffusivity maps that grow a target from a fixed central blob.
For drawn letters on 16 × 16 the regrown letters are recognisable but loose (re-simulation error 0.26–0.71), and the kill map takes the trivial route: it is lowered exactly where the letter should appear.
Only the kill rate and the overall diffusion scale are identifiable from the pattern; the feed and diffusivity maps come out no better than their nominal values.

## Physics search: simpler starts without learning

Physics search drops the network.
It writes the start as a few primitives, a blob (centre, width, strength: 4 numbers) or a line (two ends, width, strength: 6 numbers), and fits them by gradient descent through the solver [@kingma2015adam; @ledimet1986variational].
Primitives are added one at a time where the misfit is largest [@mallat1993matching; @denoyelle2020sliding].
Simplicity is counted as the fewest numbers needed to write a start; on 20 held-out 16 × 16 scenes the true starts need a median of 24.

{{< include charts/physics.html >}}

Physics search therefore trades accuracy for starts two to three times simpler than the true ones.
It was tested only on scenes made by the simulator with uniform coefficients, and the gap widens with the grid (see the grid chart above): simple answers cost faithfulness.
